title: SWE-bench Science: Can Coding Agents Resolve Engineering Tasks in Science?
hook: When software is part of the scientific instrument, a bad patch corrupts the evidence. The best agent tested clears under 50% of these repo-level scientific fixes.
key_points: 119 repository-level tasks drawn from 98 GitHub repos across 20 scientific domains.
Tasks split into three paradigms: issue-driven, expert-exploratory, and engineering-integration.
Best result reported is Claude Code with Opus-5 (max) at pass@1 below 50%.
Four recurring failure modes: missing scientific knowledge, shallow exploration or surface repair, incomplete repair or integration, and failure to generalize beyond observed cases.
A paired ablation shows scientific guidance is not uniformly helpful — well-grounded context helps, misaligned context anchors the agent.
The framing: in science, a wrong patch doesn't just break behavior, it undermines the conclusions built on the code.
content_html: Xu and colleagues introduce SWE-bench Science, a repository-level benchmark of 119 tasks pulled from 98 GitHub repositories spanning 20 scientific domains. Each task falls into one of three paradigms — issue-driven, expert-exploratory, or engineering-integration — and the point is diagnosis rather than a leaderboard: existing coding-agent evaluations report aggregate success and say little about why agents fail. Even the strongest configuration tested, Claude Code with Opus-5 (max), lands below 50% pass@1.
extra_html:
What they found

The authors identify four recurring failure mechanisms: deficits in scientific knowledge or abstraction, misguided exploration and surface-level repair, incomplete repair coverage or system integration, and failure to generalize scientific knowledge beyond the cases actually observed. A paired ablation strips out explicit scientific guidance while preserving the repository and executable context, and the result cuts against intuition — well-grounded information can usefully constrain a repair and improve both average performance and token efficiency, but poorly aligned guidance induces anchoring and doesn't reliably improve exact repair success.

Why it matters

Scientific code sits inside the evidence chain, so the cost of a plausible-but-wrong patch is higher than in ordinary software. The benchmark gives that setting a testbed, and the failure taxonomy is the more transferable contribution: it turns "agents score 47%" into specific, addressable weaknesses.

related.title: NatureBench: Can Coding Agents Match Published SOTA?
related.hook: Can coding agents reproduce — even beat — published Nature results? The best one surpassed prior SOTA on just 17.8% of 90 real scientific tasks.

flashcards.prompt: Why is a failed patch in scientific software worse than an ordinary bug?
flashcards.back_html: The software is part of the instrument — a wrong fix can corrupt the evidence underlying published conclusions, not just program behavior.

flashcards.prompt: What did the paper's paired ablation find about giving agents explicit scientific guidance?

choices.text: It helps when well-grounded, but poorly aligned guidance can anchor the agent
It always improves both accuracy and token efficiency
It made no measurable difference in any setting

flashcards.explanation_html: Removing guidance while keeping repository and execution context showed scientific knowledge is not uniformly beneficial: good context constrains repair usefully, bad context induces anchoring.

flashcards.prompt: What does a sub-50% pass@1 for the best agent tell you about aggregate benchmark scores?
flashcards.back_html: Aggregate success rates hide the mechanisms — the paper's value is in naming why agents fail (knowledge gaps, shallow repair, integration, generalization), not just how often.
